No predictive complexity, label-budget or description-length comparison establishes efficiency at matched held-out error. The DAS dimension sweep compares intervention outcomes, which do not meet the efficiency criterion.

Several direction estimators are compared directly by cosine similarity within each model, with similar agreement in additional model families. This supports robustness to fitting method; model-to-model vector alignment is not evaluated.

The adjective-fitted two-means classifier transfers well to held-out adjectives and verbs, but sentiment-bearing adverb prompts produce many chance-level results and layer-dependent successes. These materially different outcomes warrant mixed moderate evidence. Failure concerns this frozen classifier; no adverb-specific refit establishes that native sentiment information is absent.

Positive/negative ordering of a binary sentiment score does not test preservation of an independently specified sentiment metric or operation. The experiments establish classification and intervention effects without that structural comparison.

Direction-specific mean ablations reduce selected-correct SST and IMDB accuracy, with random-direction and token-position controls. Multiple removal tests strongly support necessity for the measured fidelity, although all-token/all-layer edits do not establish complete removal selectivity.

Direction swaps reverse predictions on held-out toy prompts and selected SST phrases; addition shifts generated sentiment. Multiple direct interventions support predicted changes under their reported backgrounds, with incomplete effects on natural text.

Direction-only path patching, directional ablation, and an identified toy sentiment circuit connect the direction to part of ordinary signal transmission. Restricted examples, frozen attention in some interventions, and an incomplete transformation account support limited mechanistic evidence, not a complete reconstruction.

Released primary code fits affine PCA/PLS regressions on train and scores the development split; disjoint released entity sets confirm that evaluation examples are held out from estimator fitting. Moderate evidence reflects variation across numeric properties, development-based component selection, and shared label preprocessing in the release. The PDF defines the target as the quantity expressed by the model; the example configuration uses a transformed numeric target.

PCA and PLS regression curves compare the same target and activation examples using component count as a common predictive-complexity measure, with PLS reaching comparable development performance using few components across properties and models. Released code confirms held-out estimator scoring. Shared label preprocessing and component selection limit claims about untouched test performance; intrinsic dimensionality is a separate question.

Finding predictive subspaces in several models does not measure agreement between independently fitted directions or subspaces. The paper reports fit and intervention performance without a structural reproducibility comparison.

The held-out entities come from the sampled property-specific population. No frozen probe is evaluated across prompt paraphrases, languages, domains or new value ranges, and different properties require separate fits.

Held-out PLS projections preserve ordered numeric relations, and signed direction changes produce graded, often monotonic changes in expressed values. These restricted ordering and operation tests support moderate correspondence. High regression R² alone would be insufficient, and ordering does not establish exact distances or constant arithmetic increments.

The interventions add property-directed patches and measure changed outputs. They do not selectively remove the candidate information and compare the resulting loss of the original numeric-answer behavior.

Signed edits often produce the predicted increase or decrease in expressed numeric values across properties and models. Target effects vary, and many other properties also change substantially; these materially condition-dependent target and specificity outcomes support mixed strong evidence for the reported intervention policy.

PLS directions and output trajectories are not a model of the transformations that retrieve or generate numeric attributes. The paper provides no reconstructed computation predicting both ordinary outputs and intervention effects.

Validation-selected multinomial probes predict human survey answer distributions on unseen questions across models and demographic groups. The learned objects are affine response scores followed by fixed softmax normalization. These categorical distribution predictions supply strong decoding evidence, without asserting that every opinion is encoded by a shared scalar direction.

Matched logistic-versus-MLP comparisons use the same questions and response distributions and find small KL differences across models and answer counts, despite the MLP having many more trainable parameters. This common parameter-count comparison supports strong predictive-efficiency evidence.

Layer, model and SAE-configuration sweeps compare predictive performance or feature F1. They do not compare fitted probe directions or matched SAE subspaces, so reproducibility of representation structure is untested.

Prompt-format and non-US analyses reproduce performance after applying the probing procedure again. The paper does not document frozen coefficients or direct alignment across these changes, so invariance is not established.

Predicting answer probabilities and identifying group-selective SAE features does not test a specified metric or operation on opinion space. No target-relation preservation comparison is reported for these candidate directions.

The steering protocol combines removal of base-group features with insertion of scaled source features. It does not isolate candidate removal and measure loss of the original behavior with other information preserved.

Replacing selected demographic SAE features, with scale tuned on separate question keys, reduces held-out KL to another group prompt’s model distribution. The source target is the model distribution, independently of the human-survey target used for D/E. Eligibility restrictions and variable group effects support moderate control evidence. Conflicting printed aggregate means are not used for the rating or replacement summary.

Group-selective features and steering localize causal influences but do not reconstruct how group and question information become an answer distribution. No proposed computation is validated jointly on ordinary inputs and interventions.

Affine sine/cosine probes decode held-out categorical digit labels across models and layers. Nearest-angle decoding of equally spaced anchors is equivalent to affine class scores with fixed argmax, so it satisfies the categorical D convention. This does not claim an affine scalar estimate of digit magnitude or of the complete number.

Alternative numerical bases and linear-versus-circular probes are compared for accuracy, but the paper reports no complexity or label-efficiency advantage for an affine probe at matched performance or description length.

The two models exhibit similar digit patterns, but learned directions or subspaces are not aligned across model fits, seeds or samples. Repeated accuracy and visualization patterns do not establish the rubric’s structural agreement.

A fixed probe trained on numeral tokens is applied to number words, reaching 68.6% digit accuracy at one selected layer in Llama. This is limited evidence for word-form transfer, qualified by the small value range, selected layer, and partial performance.

Native number-activation PCA and digit-group mean PCA show qualitatively ordered arcs independent of supervised sine/cosine fitting. Digit-plane reversal also tests a specified cyclic operation, but uses a replacement scale of 19 and achieves only 10–15% exact control. Together these support restricted moderate correspondence; a supervised circle fit alone does not warrant strong evidence.

Digit reversal and amplification set a counterfactual value; they do not remove digit information and test loss of the original behavior. Redundant representations are discussed but not selectively eliminated.

The fitted digit-plane intervention predicts a five-step cyclic digit change in a copying task, obtaining 10–15% exact success and higher approximate success. Scale-19 replacement, redundant digit information, and limited exact control warrant limited support under the reported policy.

The paper identifies digit geometry and changes outputs through intervention, but does not model the transformations that perform arithmetic or reconstruct ordinary computation and intervention effects from the candidate representation.

Linear square-state classifiers predict mine/yours/empty labels on held-out Othello games with high accuracy across evaluated layers and game stages. The target is player-relative board state, not the absolute black/white labels used in a less successful earlier linear comparison.

The comparison with earlier nonlinear probes also changes the board-state target from absolute colors to player-relative labels. Intervention simplicity and classifier accuracy therefore do not provide a matched predictive-efficiency comparison.

Cross-layer probe similarities compare different activation sites. Under the current robustness criterion, a fixed site must be tested across fitting samples, analysis choices, or model training; cross-layer similarity alone leaves R untested.

All probe evaluations use the same random-game distribution and target definition. Stepwise accuracy and end-game interventions do not constitute a held-out frozen-probe transfer test across domains or target-preserving input changes.

Accurate square-state labels and successful tile edits do not test preservation of a specified board-state metric or algebraic operation by activation-space objects. The paper does not provide that geometric comparison.

Color flips, empty-square edits, and flipped-direction corrections set alternative board content. They do not isolate selective removal of the proposed board-state information while preserving other relevant information, so necessity remains untested.

On 1,000 test cases, target-informed direction additions reproduce counterfactual legal-move sets for color flips and tile erasures, with mean errors around 0.10 and 0.02 against null baselines around 2.7. Additional flipped-state and endgame tests support strong reported-policy sufficiency. The metric is top-N legal-move error; coefficient selection is not sufficiently documented to claim prespecified exact control.

The first-layer attention analysis composes embedding and value/output weights to predict an empty-square direction and checks ordinary attention contributions and board-state accuracy. This explains part of the empty-square computation. Board updates and the complete transformation from board state to legal-move probabilities are unresolved, supporting limited mechanistic evidence.

Centroid fitting, PCA projections and spline interpolation do not evaluate a fitted affine predictor on an independent labeled test sample. Enumeration of concept values alone does not establish held-out decodability.

The paper compares intervention paths and their behavioral naturalness, without comparing affine predictors against alternatives at matched held-out error or training-label cost. These steering results do not test predictive efficiency.

Different domains receive separately constructed manifolds, and pullback paths are optimized against behavioral targets. Neither analysis measures agreement of directions or subspaces across repeated sample selection, fitting choices or model training.

Each concept domain and learned graph receives its own fit. The study does not freeze a predictor for transfer or measure agreement between independently identified structures across a specified target-preserving distribution change.

Fitted activation and output manifolds preserve cyclic or sequential ordering and show related geodesic distances across clean domains. Label-informed fitting and interpolation through observed centroids qualify these as direct restricted correspondence tests; neither a general discovery of intrinsic geometry nor held-out affine decoding is established.

Path interventions replace activations to induce concept transitions. The study does not selectively remove candidate concept information and compare resulting behavioral loss with a matched unedited baseline.

Setting points on the fitted manifold induces ordered output transitions across base prompts. This supports restricted moderate sufficiency for the edited state. Appendix A.6 and release path modes also show different backgrounds: manifold edits preserve the residual outside the 64-PC subspace, whereas the raw straight-path baseline replaces the whole activation. Their difference cannot be attributed to geometry alone.

Output-optimized pullback paths and manifold steering identify edited states associated with desired outputs. They do not test an account of the model transformations that construct those states during ordinary computation, leaving mechanistic sufficiency untested.

The released full-dimensional Fourier script fits affine sine/cosine predictors on 80% of activation examples and computes R² on the held-out 20%, matching the PDF’s optimizer, learning rate, and epochs. This supplies moderate evidence for decoding harmonic functions of the intermediate sum. The release enumerates operands 1–200 while the pinned PDF states 1–199, and no archived result was rerun; exact scalar-value decoding is not inferred.

DAS dimension comparisons optimize intervention fidelity, and neuron sparsity concerns causal computation. Neither provides a predictive cost comparison between affine probes and alternatives at comparable held-out error.

The paper compares task-specific subspaces and Fourier probes, but does not repeat their estimation under changed samples, analysis settings or model training to quantify reproducibility of the resulting directions.

Addition-trained Fourier probes are applied unchanged to hour, month, and weekday activations, revealing the corresponding intermediate sum harmonics. Independently fitted task subspaces also show principal-angle overlap at the relevant sites. This supports moderate transfer within one model and related arithmetic tasks; weekday alignment and offsets require care.

Native neuron activation periods, Fourier sum features, counterfactual sum interchange, and parity-specific intervention errors link numerical relations to activation structure through multiple tests. Supervised circular fitting alone would not supply this strong evidence. The relation concerns an intermediate base-10 sum used by the studied arithmetic tasks.

Selective removal of the 28 addition neurons sharply reduces accuracy across numerical and cyclic tasks, with further parity-neuron removal producing predicted parity errors.
